How do you open a checking account? 🤔 

1. Choose a bank and a checking account that fits your needs.
2. Gather your required documents - you may need a government-issued ID, your personal info, and sometimes your SIN.
3. Apply online or visit a branch.
4. Make an immediate deposit if you bank requires you to.

Where can I open a checking account? 🏦 

👉🏼 Traditional Bank - TD, RBC, Scotiabank, BMO, CIBC, and National Bank. 
- Best if you want branches and full-service banking

👉🏼 No-Fee Online Bank - Simplii, Tangerine
- Best if you want to avoid monthly fees

👉🏼 High-Interest Cash Account - EQ Bank, Wealthsimple
- Best if you want to earn more interest (my personal favs)

Next Up: breaking down money terms you hear, but may not understand.

#checkingaccount #personalfinance #moneytips #savingstips #financialeducation

How should you set your chequing account up for success? ✨ 

The ways you SHOULD use it:
- receive your paycheques
- pay your bills
- make purchases with a debit card
- send e-transfers
- withdrawal cash from ATMs
- write a cheque

This account is NOT to be used as a savings account. You should keep enough money in here to cover one months worth of expenses, plus a little buffer. 

- You won’t make interest on this money the way a savings account will, and you’re more likely to spend the money you see in this account.
- I would recommend setting up direct deposit for your paycheques to land in this account.
- You can also set up automatic payments for certain bills, so that they are taken from your account every month, and you don’t have to worry about paying a bill late.

What is a chequing account?

If you’re Canadian or British, it’s a “chequing” account. 🇨🇦 

If you’re American, it’s a “checking” account. 🇺🇸 

It’s an account set up with your bank that is used for everyday banking and transactions.

👉🏼 Almost every single bank offers these accounts, with the exception of some modern digital banks.

👉🏼 This is a necessary account for everyone to have. You should have at least one.

👉🏼 You can open one on your own starting at age 16, or if you have kids, you can open one for your child at any age. You have to be there to co-sign the account.

👉🏼 These accounts are typically free for kids, teens, or students. After that, they sometimes come with a monthly fee. 

In the next video we’ll talk about the pros and cons of a chequing account!

#checkingaccount #personalfinance #moneytips #moneyeducation #financialliteracy

How to set up your savings accounts ⤵️

Transfer any excess money out of your checking account, into your savings account.

You should store your money here for savings goals like an emergency fund, christmas shopping, a vacation, etc.

Open a High Interest Savings Account instead of a regular saving account, so you can earn more interest.

You can set automatic transfers to your savings accounts if you really want to hit those goals!

Pros and cons of checking accounts ⤵️

Pros:
👉🏼 Easy access to your money in these accounts.
👉🏼 Unlimited transactions, or a high number of them.
👉🏼 Can use your debit card with these accounts.
👉🏼 Bill payment and automatic payment features.
👉🏼 Can set up direct deposit to these accounts.

Cons:
👉🏼 Can have monthly fees.
👉🏼 No, or very low interest rates, so you don’t make money on your money.
👉🏼 Some have minimum balance requirements (meaning you have to keep some money in the account at all times).
👉🏼 Can have overdraft charges.
👉🏼 Can be transaction limits on certain accounts.

Here is our method to the points game:

We love the AMEX Cobalt and put as many expenses on it as possible. When we want to book a flight, we transfer the points at a 1:1 ratio to Aeroplan (Air Canada).

When booking our flights, we always pay for the taxes/fees portion out of pocket because the value of the points isn’t as high for that part. Meaning, if a flight from Toronto to Montreal costs ~$600, we only pay ~$100 for the taxes/fees. 

So when we say “free” we really mean “extremely discounted”! 

Points also go farther when you’re flying within Canada vs flying internationally, which is why we have used our points mostly for our domestic flights.

An RRSP is a tax-sheltered investment account for Canadians. It stands for Registered Retirement Savings Plan. 

The money you contribute is tax-deductible and helps to reduce your taxable income. This lowers the amount of tax you owe at the end of the year.

You don’t pay taxes on the growth of this money, but do pay taxes when you withdraw it.
